analysis.one_liner: Repeals federal fuel economy standards for cars and light trucks.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the fuel economy standards never left committee and died when the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have wiped out the corporate average fuel economy (CAFE) standards — the federal rules requiring carmakers to sell vehicles that average a set level of fuel efficiency. Repeal would have saved manufacturers compliance costs, but drivers would pay for it at the gas pump, since without the standards new vehicles would burn more fuel than they otherwise would. The bill never got a committee vote, let alone a floor vote, and died at the end of the 113th Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Automakers, who would no longer face federal fuel-economy requirements, and fuel sellers, who would sell more gasoline as new vehicles became less efficient. Some buyers might see slightly lower sticker prices on new vehicles, but they would pay the difference back in higher fuel costs over the life of the car.

how_it_helps.text: The bill eliminates the entire corporate average fuel economy program, freeing automakers from federal requirements to average a minimum fuel efficiency across the vehicles they sell.
Repeal would end the associated regulatory paperwork, testing, and penalty obligations that the standards impose on vehicle manufacturers.

analysis.who_pays: Drivers and households, through higher gasoline spending over the life of their vehicles, since vehicles would be permitted to use more fuel.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the standards would leave drivers facing higher gasoline costs over the life of their vehicles, since manufacturers would have no requirement to keep improving mileage.

Supporters' implicit argument is that the standards raise the upfront price of new vehicles and constrain the models automakers can offer; repealing them would remove that compliance burden — but the bill offers nothing in place of the fuel savings consumers would lose.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill never became law, so no direct cost-benefit applies. Had it passed, the main cost would have fallen on consumers in the form of higher lifetime fuel spending, with savings to automakers of compliance costs. Repealing a working, well-established efficiency standard would have offered little benefit to the public while raising their costs, and it would have undone roughly a decade of efficiency gains; its main beneficiaries were carmakers that find the standards burdensome and the oil industry, which sells more fuel when cars burn more of it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, sent to committee, and assigned to a subcommittee, but no committee or floor vote was ever taken and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 19, 2013 and referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
Two days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Power, where it stayed with no further action.
The only other action was the sponsor's introductory remarks on June 28, 2013.
No vote was ever held in either chamber, and the bill died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The fuel-efficiency standards stayed on the books, so drivers keep their fuel savings and the automakers and fuel sellers who sought repeal gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Roger Williams
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the CAFE standards and delivered introductory remarks on it.

sides.party_line_note: All 31 cosponsors were Republicans, and the sponsor was a Republican; no Democratic support is recorded.

industries.note: Repeal would have freed automakers from federal fuel-economy requirements, cutting their compliance costs, at the expense of the fuel savings the standards deliver to car buyers. The bill died, so nothing changed.
Less efficient vehicles burn more fuel, so repeal would have increased gasoline consumption and sales — a gain for fuel sellers paid for by drivers at the pump. The bill never advanced.
Without the standards, new vehicles would be expected to use more gasoline than the rules require, raising what households spend on fuel over the life of a car.
